1.pericope_label: Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the Lord
debates: What the two titles given to Pashur mean together
Whether the blow was a private assault or a legal punishment
Why God allowed a priest of his own appointing to do this
outliers: Ellicott takes the two titles as combined to imply that Pashur held the full powers of the higher office as a deputy, though some invert the relation and make him chief warden
Ellicott holds the word for smote implies a blow struck with the hands of the priest rather than the legal scourging; Gill allows either that or a scourging by an officer
Calvin frames the episode as a trial of faith, since the authority of the priests was founded on the law and the divine decree
Henry observes that the greatest malignity against the prophets was found among those who professed sanctity and concern for the church
themes: A complaint compared to that of Job, milder and more dolorous
A body held crooked all night at a conspicuous gate
A persecutor of the same priestly order as his victim
Eastern poetry warned against being read too literally

3.pericope_label: And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then said Jeremiah unto him, The Lord hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib
debates: Whether the terror is inward or the invading army
What the older name signified
In what sense the name is changed
outliers: Gill offers both an inward terror of conscience and the Chaldean army; Ellicott presses for the inward, making the man the centre from which terrors radiate as well as converge
Ellicott thinks it scarcely necessary to hunt a special sense in the older name, but reports conjectural etymologies giving joy round about, or freedom
Wesley insists the change is not that men would stop using the old name but that his condition would no longer answer it
Ellicott identifies the new name as a quotation from a psalm and guesses the psalm had been the comfort of the prophet through the night in the stocks
themes: A rare word for fear found only once outside this prophet
A phrase that became a burden, recurring three times later
Courage said to be cheap after victory and costly before it
A man made a spectacle to himself

5.pericope_label: And thou, Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house shall go into captivity: and thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there
debates: What the word rendered strength means
Why burial is announced as a punishment
What lies Pashur had prophesied
outliers: Calvin surveys four ancient renderings of the word, strength, substance, citadels and riches, and derives it from a root meaning to be strong
Calvin answers the difficulty of burial by distinguishing the place, Babylon being set against a land in which burial was itself a pledge of the inheritance
Ellicott infers that Pashur was among those who urged resistance on the hope of an alliance with Egypt, though the predictions are not recorded
Keil and Delitzsch divide what follows into a complaint that passes into a cry of hope and a cursing of the day of his birth
themes: Wealth got by long labour said to be mourned more than wealth inherited
A family led away as a public proof that its head was an impostor
Priests of the same section found in numbers at Babylon afterwards
A clamour raised a hundred times and disregarded

7.pericope_label: O Lord, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me
debates: Whether the complaint is sincere or ironical
How the verb rendered deceived should be translated
In what the prophet supposed himself deceived
outliers: Calvin holds the language ironical, the prophet assuming the character of enemies who charged him with foretelling a ruin that would never come, and rejects both a hasty-impulse reading and a harsher one
Clarke calls the received translation exceptionable and irreverent, since the verb means to persuade or allure, and quotes an old version giving thou leddest me aside
Ellicott reads the Lord as appearing to the prophet like a hard taskmaster who forced him into a work he shrank from and gave him scorn as his only wage
Gill and Henry both describe the words as a struggle between grace and corruption under temptation
themes: Enemies said to make war on heaven while thinking they oppose a man
An old version reading thou leddest me aside
Good men called but men at the best
A promise of rule over nations found to mean his own people

8.pericope_label: But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay
debates: What the two cries of the eighth verse mean
Why the prophet could not keep silent
Whether the resolution to stop was spoken or inward
outliers: Ellicott shows the two verbs are different words, the first a cry of complaint and the second a cry of protest
Calvin sets aside as too frigid the reading that the prophet merely complained of his own treatment, and prefers that the wickedness of the people compelled severity
Ellicott recovers an echo lost in English, the verb of I could not stay being the same as the prevailed of the previous verse
Gill and Wesley both insist the resolution to be silent was made in the heart and never spoken
themes: Crying aloud in tranquil times called mad affectation
A fire in the hollow of the bones burning the marrow
Refusing a call said to be as dangerous as running without one
A temptation described as besetting ministers generally

10.pericope_label: But the Lord is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail
debates: Whether the tenth verse gives a reason to stop prophesying or to continue
Who is addressed in the words report and we will report
How the last clause should be rendered
outliers: Gill records the disagreement over the function of the verse and rejects a rendering that would keep the new name untranslated, since neither the accents nor the number will bear it
Ellicott holds the words are spoken by the persecutors to each other rather than to the prophet, and renders do you report
Ellicott and Wesley both prefer because they have not dealt wisely to they shall not prosper
Keil and Delitzsch take fear on every side as a proverbial expression for a harassed condition rather than a particular reference
themes: Great men who sat still and sent others to gather evidence
Familiars defined as every man of my peace
The word for enticed shown to be the word earlier rendered deceived
God called a brazen wall, on condition that we are sure he is on our side

12.pericope_label: Sing unto the Lord, praise ye the Lord: for he hath delivered the soul of the poor from the hand of evildoers
debates: What the trying of the righteous means
Who is summoned to join the praise
What the poor and the soul stand for
outliers: Calvin makes the appeal to the searcher of hearts the proof that the prophet did not falsely pretend the name of God, since he dared to make him witness and judge of his own integrity
Gill reads the trying either as vindicating the cause of the righteous or as testing their faith and patience and finding their affections real
Calvin corrects two words, the poor meaning not one in low circumstances but one helpless and defenceless, and the soul meaning the life
Gill reports an opinion that the summons is addressed to the saints then in Jerusalem who wished the prophet well
themes: Many wrappings and coverings said to lie over the recesses of the heart
A cry out of the depths ending in praise
Deliverance felt while the circumstances remain unchanged
Distress said to be needed before the power of God can be acknowledged

14.pericope_label: Cursed be the day wherein I was born: let not the day wherein my mother bare me be blessed
debates: Whether these verses stand in their proper place
Whether the curse is sin or infirmity
Who the messenger of the birth was
outliers: Clarke holds the verses are displaced and conjectures their proper place between the eighth and ninth, transpositions in this prophet being frequent
Calvin denies both dislocation and a new temptation, and reads the passage as a retrospective amplification of the thanksgiving, showing the depth from which the deliverance came
Calvin refuses to extenuate the words and says the prophet most grievously sinned in becoming calumnious toward God, while Ellicott declines to apportion praise or blame at all
Gill reports and dismisses an opinion that the prophet knew the messenger to have been Pashur
themes: An old English version rendering the man child a knave child
The crown of sorrow found in remembering happier days
A curse assuming that life has never been a blessing
A reader advised to reverence, to sympathise and to be silent

16.pericope_label: Wherefore came I forth out of the womb to see labour and sorrow, that my days should be consumed with shame?
debates: Who was to have slain the prophet in the womb
Whether the imprecation can be excused
How the last verse should be rendered
outliers: Gill reports three answers, God, the angel of death, or the messenger, and prefers the messenger, so that the curse is for not committing murder
Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion on grammatical grounds, the subject of the verb being logically the man on whom the curse falls
Calvin refuses the excuse, since the prophet was created to sorrow and trouble as all are, and many with an honourable testimony from God had suffered reproach before him
Ellicott declines to smooth the passage, finding thought, structure and even grammar alike significant of intense emotion in their abruptness
themes: Noises in the night said to take full possession where daylight alarms do not
A man cursed for not having committed a murder
Heaven and earth mingled by a single frenzy
Grammar itself read as evidence of feeling
